name: The papal-imperial power struggle under Innocent III and Frederick II
plain_explanation: Innocent III pushed the medieval papacy's claims to temporal supremacy further than any pope before him, securing formal submission from England, Portugal, and Aragon, and installing his own ward, the young Frederick II, as Emperor. But Frederick grew into a formidable, culturally brilliant but politically reactionary ruler whose decades-long conflict with successive popes -- fueled by his refusal to crusade promptly, his negotiated (rather than military) recovery of Jerusalem, and his ambitions in Italy -- ended in stalemate at his death, with the papacy narrowly triumphant but at lasting cost to its moral authority.
precise_definition: The extended thirteenth-century conflict between the papacy (Innocent III and his successors) and the Holy Roman Empire (chiefly Frederick II), fought over control of Italy, the Sicilian kingdom, Crusading obligations, and ultimate sovereignty between spiritual and temporal power.
why_it_mattered: It represents the political culmination of the conflict traced through the preceding two chapters, and its outcome -- papal victory over the Empire, but at the cost of moral prestige -- sets up the decline of papal authority treated in Chapter XV.
historical_origin: Begins with Innocent III's accession in 1198 and Frederick II's minority under his guardianship; intensifies after Frederick's own accession as Emperor in 1212 and continues until Frederick's death in 1250.
examples: Frederick's negotiated recovery of Jerusalem from the Muslims in 1229 while still under excommunication, angering the Pope more than his earlier refusal to crusade at all
Frederick's new legal code for Sicily, minting of 'augustals' (the first Western gold coinage in centuries), and founding of the University of Naples
Frederick's mutilation and persecution of plotters, and the suicide of his former minister Pietro della Vigna after being blinded on suspicion of treachery
influence_on_later_thinkers: The political vacuum and mutual exhaustion left by Frederick's death contributed to the fragmentation of Italy and the eventual thirteenth-to-fourteenth-century decline of both imperial and (more gradually) papal power, treated further in Chapter XV.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Illustrates the thoroughly entangled character of thirteenth-century politics and religion: crusading obligation, heresy, and territorial ambition were all simultaneously religious and political instruments.
